title: Day 1 · Phase 1 — Re-anchoring: the impact answer needs energy
bodyHtml:
DAY 1 · Phase 1 — Setting up the question

Unit 3 said "big force." That's not yet a damage answer. An energy budget helps; damage also depends on material and stopping conditions.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS (preview)

K1. Work as a way energy moves. K2. Kinetic energy as the energy of motion. R4. Why 2026-XJ's KE is the load-bearing number for impact damage (preview).

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used momentum and impulse to analyze impact and deflection. This unit asks how much energy is involved and what energy accounts can establish about the fictional scenario.

How today connects:

end of Unit 3. We know 2026-XJ's momentum at impact. We know the average impact force is enormous. We don't yet have a damage estimate that matches what people actually use (Tunguska, Chicxulub) — those are reported in TNT equivalents.

Today's pivot: The number people quote for asteroid impacts is the asteroid's KINETIC ENERGY. Unit 4 builds that framework. Day 19 cashes it in.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Return Unit 3 transfer tasks. Highlight one or two strong DART analyses. "You know momentum. Now: why isn't that enough?"

5–18 min

• Demo: drop a tennis ball from waist height onto a tile. Then drop the same ball from head height. Then drop a baseball from head height. Have students rank "how much did the floor feel that?" Push: what changed between cases? (Speed. Mass. Both at once.)

18–28 min

Save an initial energy prediction before revealing K = ½mv². Then test the ratio with controlled quantities. Distinguish kinetic energy from damage, which also depends on materials and stopping conditions.

28–42 min

• Mini-lecture preview: Unit 4 is about energy. Three big payoffs: (1) cashing out the asteroid impact in TNT-equivalents (Day 19). (2) escape velocity — could 2026-XJ have ESCAPED if it had been faster? (Day 20). (3) why heat is missing energy from inelastic collisions (Day 18 / Unit 5 bridge).

42–48 min

• Individual exit: At fixed mass, doubling a cart’s speed changes its kinetic energy by what factor? Use K = ½mv² to support your answer. Compare with your initial prediction and explain why this does not prove that every measure of crash damage grows by that same factor.

48–50 min

• Marzano on K1/K2/R4 preview.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Compare the initial prediction with the final energy explanation. At fixed mass, doubling speed gives four times the kinetic energy; it does not establish a universal fourfold damage rule.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: Unit 3 transfer tasks scored; tennis ball; baseball; tile floor zone; whiteboard with a damage-ranking column.

Hewitt reading: CPA: no reading. Honors: Ch 9 §9.1.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §7.2 Kinetic Energy and the Work-Energy Theorem (pp. 290–294). Focus: Explain why the speed-squared dependence of kinetic energy adds information beyond momentum. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

• Individual exit: At fixed mass, doubling a cart’s speed changes its kinetic energy by what factor? Use K = ½mv² to support your answer. Compare with your initial prediction and explain why this does not prove that every measure of crash damage grows by that same factor.

Differentiation: ELs — sentence frame "_____ damage more because _____"; SWDs — verbal version offered; Honors extension — "what NUMBER would you make to capture 'how hard to stop' AND 'how much damage'? Hint: not mass × velocity."

A tennis ball and baseball change both mass and material. Use otherwise identical carts with added mass to isolate mass; do not treat drop sound or damage as a direct energy measurement.

CPA teaching sequence: Begin with an energy-store diagram and labeled initial/final states. Use calculator-friendly values for the first example, show one algebra move per line, and separate choosing the model from substituting numbers.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

Collect the individual evidence before the 1–3 target self-rating. Use the evidence to choose the next teaching step; completion, video viewing, and a student self-rating do not set a teacher mastery rating.

title: Day 2 · Phase 2 — Work: W = Fd
bodyHtml:
DAY 2 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

W = F·d. Units of Joules. Work is energy transferred by a force.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K1. Work definition. S1. Compute work in 1D.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used momentum and impulse to analyze impact and deflection. This unit asks how much energy is involved and what energy accounts can establish about the fictional scenario. The preceding meeting focused on Re-anchoring: the impact answer needs energy.

How today connects:

Earth's gravity does WORK on 2026-XJ as it falls — that work increases the asteroid's energy. By the time it reaches Earth, all that work has accumulated into a colossal kinetic energy.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Hand back Day 1 exit tickets. Anchor: "Today we name the quantity 'how much energy got moved.'"

5–15 min

• Direct instruction: W = F · d, where F is the force along the direction of motion. Units: Joules (N·m). Examples on the board: pushing a 100-N box 5 m → W = 500 J. Lifting a 50-N grocery bag 2 m → W = 100 J.

15–28 min

• Demonstrate ZERO work cases. Push a wall — F applied but d = 0, so W = 0. Carry a book level across the room — F is vertical (up), d is horizontal, no motion in F's direction, W = 0. (Tease tomorrow's angle case.)

28–40 min

• Group practice — 6 problems with varying F, d, and zero-work conditions. Force students to evaluate "is there motion IN THE DIRECTION OF THE FORCE?"

40–48 min

• Exit ticket: "You lift a 20-N book 1.5 m. How much work did you do? You then walk 3 m holding the book at that height. How much MORE work did you do?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on K1/S1.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check that displacement, not just elapsed effort, appears in work. For the parallel-force case, students should report joules and identify the force acting on the chosen object.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: a book, a wall to push on, a small box, packet practice problems.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 9 §9.1. Honors: Ch 9 §9.1–9.2.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §7.1 Work: The Scientific Definition (pp. 287–290). Focus: Identify the force component along displacement; distinguish scientific work from effort. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on zero-work: when students say "I did work — I felt tired carrying the book" — push: "Did the book RISE while you walked? Was force aligned with motion? Where did your tiredness come from?" Distinguish biological energy from mechanical work.

Differentiation: ELs — visual showing F arrow + d arrow with alignment; SWDs — pre-printed evaluation checklist ("Is F nonzero? Is d nonzero? Is F along d?"); Honors extension — "if you carry the book UP the stairs, are you doing work? On what?"

CPA teaching sequence: Begin with an energy-store diagram and labeled initial/final states. Use calculator-friendly values for the first example, show one algebra move per line, and separate choosing the model from substituting numbers.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. title: Day 3 · Phase 2 — Work at an angle + negative work
bodyHtml:
DAY 3 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

W = F·d·cos θ. Friction does NEGATIVE work. Lifting against gravity does positive work.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K1. Work with angle. R1. Reason about sign of work.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used momentum and impulse to analyze impact and deflection. This unit asks how much energy is involved and what energy accounts can establish about the fictional scenario. The preceding meeting focused on Work: W = Fd.

How today connects:

If 2026-XJ enters the atmosphere, air friction does NEGATIVE work on it — taking energy away. (Hence: shooting stars glow as their KE converts to heat + light.)

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Quick check: W = F·d. Units?

5–18 min

• Direct instruction: when F is at angle θ to motion, only the COMPONENT of F along d does work. W = F·d·cos θ. When θ = 0 → W = F·d (full work). When θ = 90° → W = 0 (no work). When θ between 90° and 180° → W < 0 (negative work, energy taken AWAY).

18–32 min

• Worked example: pulling a 100-N suitcase 10 m at a 30° angle above horizontal. W = 100·10·cos30° = 866 J. Then: friction force 20 N opposing motion. W_friction = 20·10·cos180° = -200 J. Net work = 666 J.

32–42 min

• Group practice — 4 problems mixing angles and signs.

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "You push a 30-N box 4 m across the floor at constant speed against 12 N of friction. What work did YOU do? What work did friction do? What's the NET work?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on K1/R1.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check the angle between force and displacement. Positive, negative, and zero work must be justified from that relationship, not from the sign of a coordinate alone.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: Trig reference card with cos values for common angles; practice problems printed.

Hewitt reading: CPA: no reading. Honors: Ch 9 §9.1; Ch 5 §5.3.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, revisit §7.1 Work: The Scientific Definition (pp. 287–290). Focus: Determine positive, negative, or zero work from the force-displacement angle. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on negative work: when a student says "friction does work" without the negative sign, stop. "In which direction is the friction force? In which direction is motion? What's the angle? What sign does that give?"

Differentiation: ELs — diagrams pre-drawn with F and d arrows + θ labeled; SWDs — column-based worksheet (F | d | θ | cos θ | W); Honors extension — "what's the net work on a satellite in CIRCULAR orbit over one revolution? Why?" (Zero — gravity perpendicular to motion. Preview Day 9.)

CPA teaching sequence: Begin with an energy-store diagram and labeled initial/final states. Use calculator-friendly values for the first example, show one algebra move per line, and separate choosing the model from substituting numbers.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. title: Day 4 · Phase 2 — Kinetic energy + work-energy theorem
bodyHtml:
DAY 4 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

The squared speed term lands today.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K2. Kinetic energy. K4. Work-energy theorem. S2. Compute KE.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used momentum and impulse to analyze impact and deflection. This unit asks how much energy is involved and what energy accounts can establish about the fictional scenario. The preceding meeting focused on Work at an angle + negative work.

How today connects:

The DAMAGE number for asteroids is their KINETIC ENERGY at impact. Today we get the formula, then build intuition for how big asteroid KEs are.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Hook: revisit Day 1's question. "Doubling speed — does damage double?" Pose it again. Today we answer.

5–15 min

• Direct instruction: KE = ½mv². Walk through the formula. Units: Joules (kg·m²/s²). The SQUARED velocity is the load-bearing feature.

15–28 min

• Worked example sequence: KE of (a) a 1500-kg car at 30 m/s; (b) the SAME car at 60 m/s. Show that doubling v gives FOUR TIMES the KE. Repeat with (c) bullet, (d) sprinter, (e) 2026-XJ — same table as Unit 3 Day 2, now with KE instead of momentum.

28–40 min

• Work-energy theorem: the NET work done on an object equals its CHANGE in KE. W_net = ΔKE = KE_f − KE_i. Worked example: a 1-kg cart starts at rest. 10 N net force pushes it 5 m. What's its final speed?

40–48 min

• Exit ticket: "A 2-kg ball at 3 m/s has 9 J of KE. If a net work of 27 J is done on it, what's its final speed?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on K2/K4/S2.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Look for speed squared in kinetic energy and net work equal to the change in kinetic energy. Students should distinguish final KE from change in KE.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: KE-comparison table from Unit 3 Day 2 — refresh it with the KE column; calculator availability; the squared-v intuition demo ready (tennis ball at low + high speed).

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 9 §9.5. Honors: Ch 9 §9.3–9.5 + Think and Solve 46, 52.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §7.2 Kinetic Energy and the Work-Energy Theorem (pp. 290–294). Focus: Connect net work with the change in kinetic energy, keeping initial and final states explicit. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on KE quadrupling: when students are surprised, lean in. "This is why highway speeds aren't just twice as dangerous as 30 mph — they're FOUR times. Why?"

Differentiation: ELs — KE formula with each piece labeled in words; SWDs — column table for the worked examples; Honors extension — "if I'm a passenger going 60 mph and the car decelerates uniformly to 0 over 2 s, what was the work done on me by my seatbelt?"

CPA teaching sequence: Begin with an energy-store diagram and labeled initial/final states. Use calculator-friendly values for the first example, show one algebra move per line, and separate choosing the model from substituting numbers.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. title: Day 5 · Phase 2 — Work-energy theorem: worked examples
bodyHtml:
DAY 5 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

The work-energy theorem is a shortcut: skip kinematics, go straight from forces to final speed.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

S4. Apply the work-energy theorem.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used momentum and impulse to analyze impact and deflection. This unit asks how much energy is involved and what energy accounts can establish about the fictional scenario. The preceding meeting focused on Kinetic energy + work-energy theorem.

How today connects:

The asteroid's free fall toward Earth IS work done by gravity. The work-energy theorem lets us compute KE at impact from gravitational work — without ever solving for time or detailed velocity history.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Quick recap: W_net = ΔKE. Pull yesterday's example back up.

5–18 min

• Worked example 1: a 1500-kg car at 30 m/s brakes to rest. If the brakes apply 9000 N, how far does it travel? (Use W_net = -F·d = 0 − ½mv²; solve for d.)

18–32 min

• Worked example 2: a 100-kg roller-coaster car coasts down a 10-m incline. Net work done by gravity = mgh = 9800 J. What's its speed at the bottom? (Show this is FASTER than the kinematics route.)

32–42 min

• Group practice — 5 problems mixing braking, sliding, falling. Force students to identify NET work and apply ΔKE.

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "A 0.5-kg ball is fired from a spring that does 8 J of work on it. The ball starts at rest. What's its speed?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on S4. Tomorrow: lab.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check the initial and final states and all relevant work terms. A braking force does negative work on the moving object; the resulting energy change must have the same sign.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: packet practice; calculator availability; KE/W reference card.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 9 §9.6. Honors: Ch 9 §9.6 + Think and Solve 50, 54.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, revisit §7.2 Kinetic Energy and the Work-Energy Theorem (pp. 290–294). Focus: Follow a work-energy example, identify the system, and check the conclusion against a force-based approach. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on choosing the theorem: when students reach for kinematics on a complex case, push: "Do you know the FORCES? Do you know the DISTANCES? Could you just sum the work?"

Differentiation: ELs — worked example with each step in plain English; SWDs — fill-in-the-blank template (Step 1: identify W_net. Step 2: set = ΔKE. Step 3: solve for v_f.); Honors extension — "in the roller-coaster problem, friction takes 2000 J away. Now what's the bottom speed?"

title: Day 6 · Phase 2 — Vernier KE lab: measuring work-energy theorem
bodyHtml:
DAY 6 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Cart on a track, known applied force, measure final v with photogate, compare to predicted v.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

S9. Vernier energy measurement. K4. Confirm work-energy theorem experimentally.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used momentum and impulse to analyze impact and deflection. This unit asks how much energy is involved and what energy accounts can establish about the fictional scenario. The preceding meeting focused on Work-energy theorem: worked examples.

How today connects:

If W_net = ΔKE holds in our carts, we can TRUST it for any asteroid energy calculation we do later in the unit.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Lab overview + safety beat (level track, gentle pulls, photogates clamped).

5–18 min

• Teacher demo: cart on track. A known mass hanging over a pulley applies a measurable force. Photogate reads cart velocity at the end. Compute predicted v from W_net = ΔKE; compare to measured.

18–38 min

• Lab: pairs run 3 trials with different hanging masses. For each: compute W_net (force × distance), predict v_f, measure v_f, compute % difference.

38–42 min

• Class data compilation. Discuss sources of error: friction in pulley + track, mass measurement, photogate timing.

42–45 min

Individual exit: Explain one result from today using a labeled sketch, calculation, or specific observation. State the model or relationship you used and one assumption. Use your own evidence before comparing with a partner.

45–48 min

• Lab write-up start.

48–50 min

• Marzano on S9.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Compare measured net work with measured change in kinetic energy, including friction or other unmeasured work. Require a data-based claim and an uncertainty discussion.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: Vernier dynamics carts + tracks + pulleys + hanging masses; photogates + LabQuest; balance; lab write-up template.

Hewitt reading: CPA: no reading. Honors: no reading.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, revisit §7.2 Kinetic Energy and the Work-Energy Theorem (pp. 290–294); §1.3 Accuracy, Precision, and Significant Figures (pp. 27–29). Focus: Before the lab, connect measured work with the predicted kinetic-energy change; use uncertainty when evaluating agreement. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on % difference: if a group is at 12% off, push: "What in the setup did NEGATIVE work that we didn't count? Friction. Estimate it."

title: Day 7 · Phase 2 — Gravitational PE near Earth: U = mgh
bodyHtml:
DAY 7 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

U_g = mgh. The energy stored by lifting against gravity. Reference height matters.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K3. Gravitational PE near Earth's surface. S3. Compute PE.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used momentum and impulse to analyze impact and deflection. This unit asks how much energy is involved and what energy accounts can establish about the fictional scenario. The preceding meeting focused on Vernier KE lab: measuring work-energy theorem.

How today connects:

2026-XJ has gravitational PE relative to Earth. As it falls, that PE converts to KE. The PE is the "battery" the asteroid spends as it gets closer.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Hook: "Where does a ball get its KE when it falls? It had energy BEFORE it fell. What kind?"

5–18 min

• Direct instruction: U_g = mgh (near Earth). Show the derivation: work done LIFTING a mass m up a height h against gravity = mg·h. That work is stored as PE.

18–28 min

• Reference height: PE depends on the CHOICE of zero. Choose ground = 0 → top has PE. Choose top = 0 → ground has -PE. Only the DIFFERENCE matters physically.

28–40 min

• Worked examples: PE of a 70-kg person at the top of a 100-m building (relative to street). PE of a 0.5-kg book on a 1.2-m table (relative to floor). PE of a 50-kg cart at the top of a 8-m ramp.

40–48 min

• Exit ticket: "A 2-kg book on a desk 1.0 m above the floor. What's its PE relative to the floor? Relative to the desktop?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on K3/S3.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check the selected zero-height reference and the vertical height change. Students should explain why a different reference changes PE values but not the predicted change.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: packet practice; calculator availability; a tall object (broomstick) to show "height matters relative to what."

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 9 §9.4. Honors: Ch 9 §9.4 + Think and Solve 47, 51.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §7.3 Gravitational Potential Energy (pp. 295–300). Focus: Choose a gravitational potential-energy reference and apply mgh only where the gravitational field is approximately constant. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on reference height: when a student insists their answer is "the right one," stop. "Both answers are right relative to a different reference. Which one matters depends on where the object will eventually FALL TO."

Differentiation: ELs — visual with PE values at multiple heights showing reference matters; SWDs — pre-printed problems with reference height stated explicitly; Honors extension — "if I'm on a tall building, is U = mgh accurate? When does it break? (When g changes with altitude — preview Day 9.)"

title: Day 8 · Phase 2 — When mgh fails: g changes with altitude
bodyHtml:
DAY 8 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

mgh assumes g is constant. For an asteroid 100,000 km out, g is NOT 9.8.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K3. Limits of mgh. Preview to universal PE.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used momentum and impulse to analyze impact and deflection. This unit asks how much energy is involved and what energy accounts can establish about the fictional scenario. The preceding meeting focused on Gravitational PE near Earth: U = mgh.

How today connects:

If we tried to compute 2026-XJ's PE relative to Earth using mgh with g=9.81, we'd get a hilariously wrong answer. Tomorrow we get the right formula.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Quick check: U_g = mgh. Conditions?

5–18 min

• Probe: "What's the PE of a 1000-kg object at 100,000 km altitude using mgh?" Have students compute. Then: "What's g at 100,000 km altitude?" (From Unit 2: g = GM/r² → about 0.04 m/s².) The mgh formula assumed g = 9.81. The error is HUGE.

18–30 min

• Bridge: we need a PE formula that USES g(r). Set up: PE comes from integrating work done by gravity along the radial direction. Without calculus, just announce the result: U_g = -GMm/r.

30–42 min

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Recap: KE = ½mv². PE = mgh (near surface) or -GMm/r (general).

32–42 min

• Group practice — 4 problems mixing dropped-from-height, sliding-down-ramp, pendulum-swing. Each uses KE + PE = const.

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "A 0.2-kg ball is dropped from 1.8 m. What's its speed at impact?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on K5.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Require a stated system and conservation condition. If mechanical energy decreases, students must account for transfer to other energy stores or across the system boundary.

DAY 17 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Compute KE_before vs KE_after for elastic + inelastic. Where does the missing energy go?

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

R2. Track energy transformations through collisions.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used momentum and impulse to analyze impact and deflection. This unit asks how much energy is involved and what energy accounts can establish about the fictional scenario. The preceding meeting focused on Power: how fast work gets done.

How today connects:

Asteroid impact = perfectly inelastic. The asteroid's KE doesn't disappear — it converts to heat, sound, mechanical deformation, light. THAT'S the damage.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Quick check: which collision conserves both p and KE? (Elastic.) Which conserves only p? (Inelastic.)

5–18 min

• Worked example: 1-kg ball at 6 m/s strikes a 1-kg ball at rest. Compute KE_before. (a) ELASTIC: KE_after using Unit 3 Day 9 result (v₁f=0, v₂f=6). KE_after same as before. (b) PERFECTLY INELASTIC: stick together, v_f = 3 m/s (Unit 3 Day 8). KE_after = ½·2·9 = 9 J. KE_before was ½·1·36 = 18 J. HALF the energy is GONE.

18–32 min

• Where did the missing 9 J go? Lead the class to: heat, deformation, sound. The pieces stuck together — energy was spent making them stick.

32–42 min

• Group practice — 3 collision problems. Each: compute KE_before, KE_after, ΔKE. Inelastic always loses energy.

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "A 0.5-kg ball at 10 m/s strikes a 1.5-kg stationary block; they stick. How much KE was lost?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on R2. Tomorrow: HEAT is the missing energy.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Compare before-and-after momentum and kinetic energy separately. An inelastic collision can conserve total system energy while kinetic energy decreases.

TimeWhat happens

• Marzano on K8/K5. Unit 5 picks up here.

DAY 20 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

v_esc = √(2GM/r). Set KE = |U| and solve.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

This unit asks how much energy is involved and what energy accounts can establish about the fictional scenario. The preceding meeting focused on Asteroid impact yield: KE in TNT equivalents.

How today connects:

If 2026-XJ had been MOVING FASTER, it could have escaped Earth's gravity well entirely — no impact, no orbit, just fly past. The threshold is escape velocity.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Hook: "What's the SLOWEST speed at which you can throw a baseball straight up and NEVER have it come back?"

5–18 min

• Derivation: object at Earth's surface with KE = ½mv² and PE = -GMm/r. For escape, total energy must be ≥ 0 (so it reaches infinity with at least 0 KE). Set ½mv_esc² = GMm/r. Solve: v_esc = √(2GM/r).

18–30 min

• Compute Earth's escape velocity: v_esc = √(2·6.67×10⁻¹¹·6×10²⁴/6.37×10⁶) ≈ 11.2 km/s. That's 25,000 mph.

30–42 min

• Worked examples: escape velocity from Moon (much smaller). From Mars. From a 1000-km asteroid (tiny — almost nothing). What does this tell us about why small bodies don't hold atmospheres?

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "If you were on Mars, what's the escape velocity? (M_Mars = 6.4×10²³ kg, r_Mars = 3.39×10⁶ m.)"

48–50 min

• Marzano on R5/S8.

Independent. 5 multi-part problems: (1) work + work-energy theorem on a braking car; (2) roller-coaster speed at multiple points using ME conservation; (3) spring-launched projectile using ½kx² → ½mv² + mgh; (4) compute power required by an elevator; (5) asteroid impact yield IN TONS TNT + escape velocity from a given body.

Public-facing transfer: Write a public-facing explanation of the energy scale of 2026-XJ and compare the modeled response options. Distinguish an energy estimate from a prediction of damage.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Listen for explanations that cite the student’s own work and the four rubric dimensions. Check whether a revision answers a specific question, whether uncertainty is acknowledged, and whether the student can defend the model without a partner supplying it.

Compare the self-rating with the evidence when giving feedback. Record the teacher’s judgments independently; peer agreement or completion is not a mastery score.

MATERIALS & READING

Work retained from the first meeting; the same task and permitted references; calculators; four-dimension rubric; peer-feedback sheet; final reflection and submission folder.

Hewitt reading: CPA: no new reading. Honors: no new reading during assessment.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: No new OpenStax reading during the transfer assessment. Use only the references permitted in the assessment plan; revisit a focused section after feedback.

TEACHER NOTES

Assessment conventions: Use the Unit 1 rubric: Science / Reasoning / Communication / Transfer-to-Asteroid. Score the four dimensions independently from 0–4; report the profile without averaging and use the established lowest-dimension conversion. Science checks the physics; Reasoning checks the choice and justification of the model; Communication checks labeled, organized work; Transfer-to-Asteroid checks the supported connection and its limits. Peer and student ratings are feedback; the teacher makes the final judgment. Target self-ratings use the separate 1–3 scale and do not automatically become mastery ratings. Revisions follow Unit 1’s two-week window, with new evidence for a one-level move on a dimension.

Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.
